sources.name: Brysbaert, Stevens, Mandera & Keuleers (2016), How Many Words Do We Know? Practical Estimates of Vocabulary Size Dependent on Word Definition, the Degree of Language Input and the Participant's Age, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1116
sources.measures: Estimated number of English lemmas known by American native English speakers aged 20. Lemmas are uninflected words with proper nouns excluded, taken from a list of 61,800 entries. Knowledge was measured by yes/no word recognition with pseudoword correction in an online crowdsourced test.
sources.notes: n = 221,268 is the total number of individuals tested (265,346 sessions), not the age-20 American subsample, which the paper does not state in the parts read. The abstract gives the range as 27,000 lemmas (lowest 5%) to 52,000 (highest 5%). Table 4 gives the 20-year-old upper value as 51,700, and that value is used here. For 60-year-olds the paper gives a median of 48,200 lemmas and a 5th to 95th range of 35,100 to 56,400. In word families (base words) it gives a median of 11,100 at age 20 (5th to 95th: 6,100 to 14,900) and 13,400 at age 60 (9,000 to 16,700). No p99 or p99.9 is published.

definition: Estimated number of English lemmas known by American native English speakers aged 20. Lemmas are uninflected words with proper nouns excluded, taken from a list of 61,800 entries. Knowledge was measured by yes/no word recognition with pseudoword correction in an online crowdsourced test.
caveat: The question asks for the top 1% of adults, but the only source on this definition publishes no value above the 95th percentile. Its p95 for 20-year-olds is about 52,000 lemmas and for 60-year-olds 56,400 lemmas, so the true p99 lies above those figures, capped by the 61,800-lemma test list. The sample is self-selected online test takers, restricted to American native speakers and split by age. It is not a representative sample of all adults, and non-native speakers are excluded. Comparison on a different scale, not averaged: myvocab.info (BRAVE project) counts word families with an adaptive IRT test on about 29,000 self-selected native speakers. It reports p25 14,400, p50 17,100, p75 19,900 and p90 22,700 word families, with no p95 or p99. Its word-family definition differs from Brysbaert's base words, and Brysbaert's word-family median is 11,100. Older rule-of-thumb estimates (Nation; Goulden, Nation & Read 1990) put educated native speakers near 20,000 word families. Those figures are also word families and are not comparable with lemmas.

new_metric.label: English vocabulary size
new_metric.definition: The estimated number of distinct English lemmas (dictionary headwords without inflections, proper nouns excluded) a native speaker recognises as known on a word-recognition test.
